# Tobit Chapter 8 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

## Overview
Chapter 8 is theologically and narratively dense. The wedding-night scene generated disagreements in every major section: the exorcism (vv. 2-3), the prayer (vv. 5-8), Raguel's grave-digging (vv. 9-13), the doxology (vv. 14-17), and the inheritance pledge (vv. 20-21). Total divergent verses: 12 of 21.

---

## Disagreement Table

| Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | SOPHIA Resolution |
|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|-------------------|
| 8:2 | "incense ashes" vs. "ashes of the incense" | "ashes-of the incense" | "ashes of the incense" | "incense ashes" | "incense ashes" — the most natural English order; PNEUMA adopted |
| 8:3 | Geography of Asmodeus's flight | "upper-parts-of Egypt" | "upper parts of Egypt" | "far reaches of Egypt" | "upper parts of Egypt" — the GII text specifies a geographic direction, not merely distance |
| 8:4 | Address to Sarah | "Rise, sister" | "Rise up, my sister" | "Come, my sister" | "Rise, my sister" — preserves the imperative without "up" (not in Greek) and adds "my" for warmth |
| 8:7 | Central moral contrast: motive for marriage | "not on-account-of lust… but on-account-of truth" | "not out of lust… but in truth" | "not because of physical desire… honestly, with a true heart" | LOGOS: "not out of lust… but in truth" — most precise; PNEUMA's expansion of ep' aletheias into "with a true heart" is interpretive |
| 8:7 | "this my sister" (tautēn tēn adelphēn mou) | "this my-sister" | "this my sister" | "this woman as my wife" | "this my sister" — EMET/LOGOS preserve the address form; PNEUMA's substitution loses the kinship-covenant texture |
| 8:9 | Temporal framing of the night | "slept for the night" | "slept through the night" | "And they slept. Meanwhile…" | "slept through the night" — LOGOS; PNEUMA's "Meanwhile" is a narrative insertion |
| 8:10 | Raguel's fear expressed | "Perhaps he also will die" | "Perhaps he will die as well" | "What if this one dies too?" | "Perhaps he will die as well" — LOGOS; PNEUMA's interrogative shifts from reported speech to interior monologue |
| 8:11 | Concealment motivation | "that no-one may know [about it]" | "before anyone finds out" | "before anyone finds out" | LOGOS/PNEUMA agreement: "before anyone finds out" adopted |
| 8:14 | "bless" vs. "praise" in doxology | "bless you" (throughout) | "bless you" (throughout) | "praise you" | "bless you" — eulogeitosan is "bless"; "praise" represents a different Greek word (ainein) |
| 8:16 | "only children" (monogeneis) | "only-children" | "only children" | "young people who are all each other had" | "only children" — LOGOS; PNEUMA loses the monogeneis significance (echoes of Isaac, of Jephthah's daughter) |
| 8:19 | "oxen" vs. "bulls" | "oxen" | "oxen" | "bulls" | "oxen" — EMET/LOGOS; fits the feast/agricultural register; "bulls" implies young males specifically |
| 8:21 | Adoption/belonging language | "we are yours and your sister's" | "we belong to you and to your sister" | "you are our son now… this is your home" | "we belong to you and your sister" — LOGOS; PNEUMA's expansion adds adoption language not present in the Greek |

---

## Extended Notes on Key Divergences

### Verse 7 — The Heart of the Prayer
The moral contrast ep' porneia / ep' aletheias is the theological pivot of the entire book. Tobit is not a story about magic fish — it is a story about faithful love versus exploitative desire. All three agents recognized the importance of this verse, but diverged on register:

- EMET's hyphenated "on-account-of" is too syntactically heavy for a prayer.
- PNEUMA's expansion ("honestly, with a true heart") is interpretively valid but adds words not in the Greek.
- LOGOS's "out of lust… but in truth" achieves the necessary compression and moral force.

SOPHIA adopts LOGOS with the observation that "lust" (not "sexual desire" or "passion") is the right English word precisely because it carries a moral valence, which is what the Greek ep' porneia ("out of prostitution/licentiousness") intends.

### Verse 9 — The Grave
This is perhaps the most tonally daring verse in the Deuterocanon. On his daughter's wedding night, her father goes out and digs a grave for the expected corpse of her seventh husband. All three agents handled this soberly, but PNEUMA's addition of "Meanwhile" slightly softens the impact by signaling a scene shift rather than letting the actions juxtapose themselves. SOPHIA keeps the minimal LOGOS rendering.

### Verse 16 — Monogeneis
The word monogeneis ("only-begotten" or "only children") is theologically charged in Jewish and later Christian usage. It appears in the LXX for Isaac (Gen 22:2, 12, 16) and Jephthah's daughter (Judges 11:34). PNEUMA's paraphrase "young people who are all each other had" loses this resonance entirely. SOPHIA preserves "only children."

*— SOPHIA*
